q: A crystal of quartz conducts heat and refracts light slightly differently along different directions. This property of crystalline solids is called:
x: Because the particles of a crystal are arranged in a regular lattice, the spacing differs along different directions, so properties such as conductivity and refractive index depend on direction: the crystal is anisotropic. Isotropy (the same in all directions) is the property of amorphous solids.

q: While a crystalline solid is melting at its melting point, heat is still being supplied but its temperature stays constant. The heat is used to:
o: Raise the average kinetic energy of the particles
Break down the regular long-range order of the lattice
Increase the number of particles in each unit cell
x: At the melting point the supplied heat (latent heat of fusion) does work against the bonding forces and breaks down the ordered lattice; the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, does not rise until all of it has melted. Thinking the heat raises the kinetic energy contradicts the constant temperature.

q: A rubber band can be stretched to several times its length and still return to its original length. This is mainly because rubber:
o: Is made of long, coiled chain molecules that straighten when stretched and coil up again
Has a regular crystal lattice whose atoms move far apart
Is an amorphous solid with no bonds between its molecules
Has a very high Young's modulus
x: Rubber is a polymeric solid: its long chain molecules are tangled and coiled, so a pull mainly straightens them, and they coil back when released. A high Young's modulus would mean a stiff material that hardly stretches, the opposite of rubber.

q: In a body-centred cubic unit cell, one atom sits at each of the 8 corners of the cube and one atom at its centre. Each corner atom is shared equally by 8 neighbouring unit cells. The number of atoms belonging to one unit cell is:
x: Each corner atom contributes 1/8 to the cell: 8 × 1/8 = 1, and the centre atom belongs wholly to the cell, giving 1 + 1 = 2. Counting every atom fully gives 9; forgetting the centre atom gives 1.

q: Tensile strain is defined as the change in length divided by the original length. The SI unit of strain is:
x: Strain = ΔL/L is metres divided by metres, a pure ratio with no unit. N m⁻² is the unit of stress (and of the moduli), not of strain.

q: A graph of tensile stress (on the vertical axis) against tensile strain is drawn for a metal wire. The slope of the straight-line part of the graph, starting at the origin, gives the wire's:
x: In the proportional region stress/strain is constant and equals Young's modulus Y, so Y is the slope. The area under the graph, not its slope, gives the strain energy per unit volume.

q: A steel wire (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) has a cross-sectional area of 0.5 mm². What load will produce a tensile strain of 0.1% in it?
x: Strain = 0.1% = 1 × 10⁻³, so stress = Y × strain = 2 × 10⁸ Pa, and F = stress × A = 2 × 10⁸ × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 100 N. Taking 0.1% as 0.01 gives 1000 N; taking it as 0.1 gives 1 × 10⁵ N.

q: A wire obeys Hooke's law. The load on it is doubled, still within the proportional limit. The elastic potential energy stored in the wire becomes:
x: Energy stored = ½ × F × extension, and the extension is proportional to F, so the energy is proportional to F². Doubling F doubles the extension too, so the energy becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times. Forgetting that the extension also doubles gives 2 times.

q: For the same increase in pressure, the fractional decrease in volume is greatest for a gas and least for a solid. Comparing the bulk moduli, this means that:
o: Gases have the largest bulk modulus and solids the smallest
All three have the same bulk modulus
Solids have the largest bulk modulus and gases the smallest
Liquids have the largest bulk modulus
x: Bulk modulus K = Δp/(ΔV/V), so a smaller fractional volume change for the same Δp means a larger K. Solids are hardest to compress (largest K) and gases easiest (smallest K). Mixing up K with compressibility, its reciprocal, reverses the order.

q: A wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 1 mm² is made of metal with Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. It is stretched by 2 mm, within its elastic limit. The elastic energy stored in it is:
x: F = YAΔL/L = 2 × 10¹¹ × 1 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 200 N, so E = ½FΔL = ½ × 200 × 0.002 = 0.2 J. Check: energy density ½Y(strain)² = ½ × 2 × 10¹¹ × (10⁻³)² = 10⁵ J m⁻³, times volume 2 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 0.2 J. Leaving out the ½ gives 0.4 J; using 2 for the extension in metres gives 200 J.

q: Wires P and Q have the same length and the same cross-sectional area. They are joined end to end and hang vertically with a load at the bottom. The Young's modulus of P is twice that of Q. The total extension is 3 mm. The extension of P is:
x: Both wires carry the same tension, so extension e = FL/(AY) is proportional to 1/Y: e_P = ½e_Q. Then e_P + 2e_P = 3 mm gives e_P = 1 mm (and e_Q = 2 mm). Giving the stiffer wire the larger share gives 2 mm; sharing equally gives 1.5 mm.

q: According to the energy band theory, a good conductor such as copper has:
o: A wide forbidden gap between a full valence band and an empty conduction band
Overlapping valence and conduction bands, so many electrons are free to move
A forbidden gap of about 1 eV between the two bands
An empty valence band and a full conduction band
x: In metals the valence and conduction bands overlap (the conduction band is partly filled), so a very large number of free electrons are available at any temperature. A wide gap describes an insulator; a gap of about 1 eV describes a semiconductor such as silicon.

q: In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor at room temperature, the number of free electrons in the conduction band compared with the number of holes in the valence band is:
o: Zero, as there are no holes in a pure semiconductor
x: In an intrinsic semiconductor each electron that is thermally excited into the conduction band leaves exactly one hole behind, so the numbers are equal. Unequal numbers of electrons and holes need doping (n-type or p-type).

q: Trivalent impurity atoms such as gallium, added to pure germanium to make a p-type semiconductor, are called acceptor atoms because each one:
o: Accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond, creating a hole
Accepts a hole and releases a free electron
Accepts a proton from the germanium nucleus
Accepts energy and becomes an insulator
x: A trivalent atom forms only three of the four covalent bonds; it takes an electron from a neighbouring bond to complete the fourth, which leaves a hole that can move. Pentavalent atoms do the opposite: they donate a free electron (donors).

q: Pure silicon has a forbidden energy gap of about 1.1 eV. Very close to 0 K, pure silicon behaves as:
o: A good conductor, because its resistance falls as the temperature falls
An insulator, because no electrons have enough energy to cross into the conduction band
x: At 0 K there is no thermal energy to lift electrons across the 1.1 eV gap, so the valence band is full, the conduction band is empty and no current can flow: silicon is an insulator. Falling resistance with falling temperature is metallic behaviour; a semiconductor's resistance rises as it is cooled.

q: In a ferromagnetic material, the small regions in which the magnetic moments of all the atoms are lined up in the same direction are called:
x: A ferromagnet is made of tiny magnetic domains, each fully magnetised; in an unmagnetised sample the domains point in random directions, and an applied field lines them up. Unit cells describe crystal structure, and depletion regions belong to p-n junctions.

q: A ferromagnetic specimen is taken repeatedly round its hysteresis loop. The area enclosed by the loop represents:
o: The energy lost as heat per unit volume in each cycle
The magnetic flux density left when the field is removed
The field needed to demagnetise the specimen
x: The area of the B–H loop equals the energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation. The flux density left at zero field is the retentivity, and the reverse field needed to remove it is the coercivity; these are points on the loop, not its area.

q: When a superconductor is cooled below its critical temperature in a magnetic field, it pushes the magnetic field lines out of itself (the Meissner effect). In this state it behaves as:
o: An ordinary conductor with low resistance
x: Expelling all magnetic flux means the field inside is zero, which is perfect diamagnetism; this is why a small magnet can float above a cooled superconductor. Ferro- and paramagnets draw field lines in, not out.
